title: First Responder: Evidence Harvesting, RBAC Lockdown & SIEM Export Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This playbook is a compact, actionable reference for security first-responders to securely harvest evidentiary artifacts, perform emergency RBAC lockdowns, and export normalized events to the SIEM for downstream triage. It is intended for on-call engineers, security oncall, and SREs participating in initial containment and evidence collection.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to suspected compromise of production inference infrastructure, control plane access, credential exfiltration, or suspicious API/model activity.
- Assumes ability to access admin consoles (IAM, logging, cloud console), SIEM export tools, and the IR automation repo.
- Primary goals: preserve forensic integrity, minimize blast radius, enable rapid analysis, and keep service continuity where possible.

Quick escalation matrix (immediate):
1) Pager alert or Slack @security-oncall -> ack within 5 mins.
2) If suspected data exfiltration or root compromise -> notify Security Lead + SRE Lead and exec-oncall.
3) If production outage impacts customers -> page incident commander (IC) and communication lead.

Runbook: Step-by-step (first 60 minutes)
0) Triage (0-5 mins):
- Read the alert context: alert source (IDS/HIPS/cloud-detection/model-anomaly), affected resources, attacker indicators (IPs, user agents, tokens).
- Take a screenshot/copy of alert metadata. Log it to a secure incident doc (link to a new postmortem doc).

1) Short-term containment (5-20 mins):
- If attacker is active (live sessions): throttle or revoke sessions rather than immediate mass shutdown if customer impact is acceptable. Use targeted token revocation by session id when available.
- RBAC emergency change: switch to a narrow-scope deny policy for suspect principals: create a temporary deny role/policy called ir-temporary-deny-<incident-id> and attach to affected principals. Note: prefer deny-lists vs blanket removal to preserve auditability.
- If credential compromise suspected for service accounts: rotate keys, disable long-lived tokens, and attach monitoring-only policies to affected service accounts until rotated.

2) Evidence harvest (parallel, 10-45 mins):
- Preserve ephemeral memory and process artifacts if host compromise suspected (only if you have forensics tooling and trained SREs). Otherwise, capture the following remote artifacts in order of volatility:
  * Live API request traces (request id, auth token hash, caller IP, timestamp) from the API gateway
  * Inference node logs and stdout/stderr for time window +/- 15 mins around alert
  * Runtime process lists, active network connections, and kernel logs (if allowed)
  * Kubernetes audit events for the namespace and pod IDs (kubectl get events / audit export)
  * Cloud provider audit logs (IAM, VPC flow logs, console auth events) and the Redwood audit log schema export (see schema excerpt below)
  * SIEM raw event search results (export JSON) for correlated IPs, UAs, and user principals
- For each artifact collected, note collector, timestamp (UTC ISO8601), collector host, and where stored. Use immutable storage where possible (object store bucket with wORM or time-limited retention).

3) SIEM export and normalization (20-60 mins):
- Run the standard export script: ir-scripts/export_to_siem.sh --incident <id> --range "<start>..<end>". If automation fails, manually run scoped queries and export JSON.
- Normalize fields into our SIEM canonical schema: see "Audit schema (canonical)" below. The goal is to make triage queries simple: index by actor.principal, actor.email, resource.id, action, outcome, request.id, src.ip, user_agent, and probe.score.
- Push exported artifacts to the SIEM incident index and attach S3/GCS locations in the SIEM ticket.

4) Communication and tickets (ongoing):
- Create incident ticket (JIRA-SEC-<auto>) and add initial summary, timeline, and artifact links.
- Post a short summary in #security-incident (private channel) using the template below.
- Notify stakeholders per escalation matrix.

RBAC considerations and emergency patterns:
- RBAC v2 quick checklist: don’t remove principals from groups unless absolutely necessary; prefer applying deny policies or conditional blocking tied to a session or IP. This preserves intent and audit trails.
- Emergency RBAC actions (order):
  1) Apply temporary deny policy to principal.
  2) Create short-lived scoped credentials for critical automation to avoid service interruption.
  3) Revoke or rotate only affected keys; schedule full rotation if lateral movement confirmed.
- Post-incident: review RBAC changes, revert temporary denies, and codify changes as least-privilege policy updates.

Audit schema (canonical excerpt) - quick reference for evidence mapping:
- event_id: uuidv4
- timestamp: ISO8601 UTC
- source: {gateway|k8s|runtime|cloud-iam|console|auth}
- actor.principal: string (user/service principal id)
- actor.email: string (if available)
- actor.ip: ipv4/ipv6
- action: string (e.g., "token:exchange", "k8s.exec", "model:deploy", "file:read")
- resource.id: string (arn / k8s://namespace/pod/name / model-id)
- outcome: {success|failure|partial}
- request.id: trace/request id (for cross-correlation)
- user_agent: string
- extra: freeform string (escaped JSON ok)

Note: because this file is used by automation, the export script will map our native logs into the canonical keys above. If you see missing fields, add a manual mapping note in the incident ticket.

Evidence storage and chain-of-custody notes:
- Store harvested files in the incident bucket: gs://redwood-ir-artifacts/<incident-id>/ and include a checksum (sha256) for each file in the ticket.
- Never alter original log files. Work on copies and record the copy command and checksums alongside the original.
- Use signed access links and short TTLs for stakeholder access. For high-sensitivity incidents (exfiltration of customer data), escalate to legal and preserve full retention.

Automations and helper scripts (where to look):
- ir-scripts/collectors/api_harvest.py -- grabs gateway traces and pairs with request ids
- ir-scripts/rbac/temporary_deny.sh -- creates deny policies and attaches them to principals
- ir-scripts/export_to_siem.sh -- runs canonical normalization and posts to SIEM
- If automation fails, fall back to manual query templates under Confluence: /SEC/playbooks/manual-siem-queries

On-call checklist (one-line actions for responders):
- ACK alert and create incident ticket
- Snapshot alert metadata (screenshot/copy)
- Apply minimal RBAC deny to suspect principal(s)
- Export gateway traces and API logs for the time window
- Export cloud IAM console logs and VPC flow logs for correlated IPs
- Run SIEM export script; attach exports to ticket
- Communicate to #security-incident with short summary and next steps

Postmortem template (what to capture after containment):
- Incident ID, timeline (UTC) with evidence links
- Root cause hypothesis and supporting artifacts
- Actions taken (containment, RBAC changes, key rotations) with actor names and timestamps
- Evidence chain-of-custody (who collected, where stored, checksums)
- SIEM queries used and raw export references
- Customer impact and mitigations (if any)
- Follow-ups: policy changes, automation improvements, RBAC audit tasks, and owners + deadlines
- Severity and lessons learned (concrete measurable items)

Communication templates (copy/paste):
- Slack short incident open: "[INC-<id>] Security oncall: investigation started for alert <alert-id>. Suspect principals: <list>. Containment in progress. No customer-facing impact identified so far. IC: <name>."
- Exec brief (1-2 lines): "Security incident <id> detected on <service>. Containment started; next update in 60 mins. No confirmed data exfiltration at this time."

Forensics escalation and legal involvement:
- If PII or customer data exposure is suspected, pause log deletion and notify Legal and Compliance immediately. Tag evidence with sensitivity="PII" and preserve full retention.

Appendix: common IR pitfalls (do not do)
- Do not do wholesale account deletions — this obliterates audit context.
- Don’t run destructive forensic commands on hosts unless that is the documented forensic path and you have approval.
- Avoid sending unredacted logs into public channels; always use the private incident channel and redact any customer identifiers unless legal asks for full copies.

Contact and resources:
- Security oncall rotation: see Confluence /SEC/oncall-schedule
- IR automation repo: github.com/redwood-inference/ir-scripts
- SIEM runbook and query library: confluence://SEC/siem-queries

Document history:
- 2025-01-15: Draft by Aisha Patel
- 2025-01-28: Added RBAC emergency patterns (Miguel Torres)
- 2025-02-03: Clarified SIEM normalization steps and canonical schema (Samira Klein)

End of playbook.
